questions.stem: A 64 year old former bus driver has 2 years of breathlessness climbing stairs and a cough with white sputum every morning through the winter. He has smoked 20 a day for 45 years. He has never had asthma or hay fever. There is a prolonged expiratory phase with scattered wheeze. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.61.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Smoker over 40 + chronic productive cough + persistent obstruction = COPD. Why not Asthma? Adult onset in a heavy smoker with no atopy and fixed obstruction favours COPD.

steps.x: Over 40, heavy smoker, exertional breathlessness, chronic productive cough, ratio below 0.7.

elim: Adult onset in a heavy smoker with no atopy and fixed obstruction favours COPD.
Large volumes of purulent sputum and coarse crackles.
Orthopnoea, oedema and crackles, not fixed obstruction.
Restrictive with fine crackles and clubbing.

steps.x: **C. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.** Smoker over 40 + chronic productive cough + persistent obstruction = COPD.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has progressive breathlessness on exertion and a chronic cough. She has never smoked cigarettes, but cooked over an open wood fire indoors for 30 years before moving to the UK. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.63.
questions.q: Which risk factor is most likely to explain her condition?
questions.e: Smoking is the main risk, but air pollution and occupational exposures also cause COPD. Why not Asbestos exposure? Causes pleural plaques, mesothelioma and fibrosis.

clues: open wood fire indoors for 30 years
steps.x: Never-smoker with decades of indoor smoke and fixed obstruction.

elim: Causes pleural plaques, mesothelioma and fibrosis.

steps.x: **B. Biomass smoke exposure.** Smoking is the main risk, but air pollution and occupational exposures also cause COPD.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with a 60 pack-year smoking history is breathless at rest. He sits leaning forward with his hands on his knees. There is central cyanosis, use of accessory muscles, a barrel-shaped chest and quiet breath sounds throughout.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: COPD signs: hyperinflation, reduced breath sounds, accessory muscle use, cyanosis. Why not Pneumonia? Fever and focal signs such as bronchial breathing.

steps.x: Heavy smoker, cyanosis, accessory muscles, hyperinflation, reduced breath sounds.

elim: Fever and focal signs such as bronchial breathing.
Sudden onset with a clear chest.
Fine crackles and a small, not hyperinflated, chest.

steps.x: **A. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.** COPD signs: hyperinflation, reduced breath sounds, accessory muscle use, cyanosis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with known COPD has 3 days of worsening breathlessness. Her usually white sputum is now green and thick, and she is wheezier. Her temperature is 37.6°C, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with no consolidation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Exacerbation: worse breathlessness, purulent sputum and wheeze. Why not Community-acquired pneumonia? The chest X-ray shows no consolidation.

steps.x: Worse breathlessness, purulent sputum, wheeze, no consolidation.

elim: The chest X-ray shows no consolidation.
Pulmonary oedema on X-ray and crackles.
Sudden pain and a visible lung edge on X-ray.

steps.x: **C. Infective exacerbation of COPD.** Exacerbation: worse breathlessness, purulent sputum and wheeze.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with COPD has 3 days of increased breathlessness, wheeze and a change in sputum from white to green. His temperature is 37.7°C and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows no consolidation. Sputum Gram stain shows small Gram-negative coccobacilli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Haemophilus influenzae is the most common cause of infective COPD exacerbations. Why not Klebsiella pneumoniae? Gram-negative rods, typically alcoholics with upper lobe pneumonia.

steps.x: COPD exacerbation, Gram-negative coccobacilli.

elim: Gram-negative rods, typically alcoholics with upper lobe pneumonia.
Has no cell wall and does not Gram stain.
Gram-negative rods, in bronchiectasis and CF.

steps.x: **A. Haemophilus influenzae.** Haemophilus influenzae is the most common cause of infective COPD exacerbations.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with severe COPD is seen in clinic at her usual level of breathlessness. She is alert. Arterial blood gas on air shows pH 7.37, PaO2 8.1 kPa, PaCO2 6.9 kPa and HCO3- 31 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
questions.e: Chronic hypoventilation with renal compensation: normal pH, high CO2, high HCO3-. Why not Acute respiratory acidosis? The pH is normal, so compensation has occurred.

steps.x: Normal pH, raised CO2 and bicarbonate in stable COPD.

elim: The pH is normal, so compensation has occurred.
The primary problem is a raised CO2.

steps.x: **B. Compensated respiratory acidosis.** Chronic hypoventilation with renal compensation: normal pH, high CO2, high HCO3-.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with COPD was given 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask by paramedics. An hour later he is drowsy with a flapping tremor and bounding pulse. ABG shows pH 7.24, PaO2 14.8 kPa and PaCO2 10.1 kPa.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Drowsy COPD patient with high CO2 = type 2 respiratory failure, an emergency. Why not Type 1 respiratory failure? His CO2 is raised.

steps.x: Drowsy COPD patient, high-flow oxygen, high CO2, acidosis.

elim: Flap occurs, but the blood gas explains his drowsiness.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 respiratory failure.** Drowsy COPD patient with high CO2 = type 2 respiratory failure, an emergency.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with severe COPD suddenly becomes very breathless and distressed. Her pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 78/44 mmHg and oxygen saturation 80%. The trachea is deviated to the left and breath sounds are absent on the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tension pneumothorax is a COPD complication: needle thoracocentesis now, without waiting for imaging. Why not Large right bulla? Bullae can mimic pneumothorax on imaging but do not cause tracheal shift and shock.

clues: trachea is deviated to the left
steps.x: Sudden collapse, hypotension, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds.

elim: Bullae can mimic pneumothorax on imaging but do not cause tracheal shift and shock.
Does not cause unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.
Causes shock but no tracheal deviation.

steps.x: **E. Tension pneumothorax.** Tension pneumothorax is a COPD complication: needle thoracocentesis now, without waiting for imaging.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with long-standing COPD has 3 months of worsening ankle swelling. His JVP is raised by 6 cm, there is a left parasternal heave and pitting oedema to the knees. His oxygen saturation is 87% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic hypoxia drives pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale). Why not Left ventricular failure? Causes orthopnoea and bibasal crackles; his signs are right-sided.

steps.x: Chronic hypoxia, raised JVP, parasternal heave, oedema.

elim: Causes orthopnoea and bibasal crackles; his signs are right-sided.
Rare; Kussmaul's sign and pericardial calcification.

steps.x: **B. Cor pulmonale.** Chronic hypoxia drives pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with severe COPD and chronic hypoxaemia attends clinic. She is plethoric. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 192 g/L and haematocrit 0.58. Her white cells and platelets are normal and she has no splenomegaly.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her blood count?
questions.e: Polycythaemia is a COPD complication from chronic hypoxia (EPO drive). Why not Polycythaemia vera? Raises white cells and platelets with splenomegaly.

steps.x: Chronic hypoxia, isolated raised Hb, no splenomegaly.

elim: Raises white cells and platelets with splenomegaly.
Very high white cells and splenomegaly.

steps.x: **E. Secondary polycythaemia from chronic hypoxia.** Polycythaemia is a COPD complication from chronic hypoxia (EPO drive).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with severe COPD and chronic hypoxia has an ECG before surgery. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history. The ECG shows a tall peaked P wave in lead II and a dominant R wave in V1.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his ECG axis?
o: Indeterminate axis from left bundle branch block
questions.e: Long-standing hypoxia causes RV hypertrophy with right axis deviation. Why not Left axis deviation? Seen in left anterior hemiblock or LVH.

steps.x: Chronic hypoxia, P pulmonale, dominant R in V1.

elim: Seen in left anterior hemiblock or LVH.
RV hypertrophy shifts the axis right.
LBBB is not the COPD pattern.

steps.x: **E. Right axis deviation.** Long-standing hypoxia causes RV hypertrophy with right axis deviation.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman who has smoked for 40 years has had 4 chest infections in 2 years. She now has breathlessness walking 200 metres, a daily cough with mucus and reduced exercise tolerance. Examination shows rhonchi and a hyperinflated chest.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: COPD: chronic productive cough, frequent infections, rhonchi and hyperinflation. Why not Bronchiectasis? Daily large volumes of purulent sputum, coarse crackles and often clubbing.

steps.x: Smoker, frequent infections, mucus, rhonchi, hyperinflation.

elim: Daily large volumes of purulent sputum, coarse crackles and often clubbing.
Hilar lymphadenopathy, often in young adults.

steps.x: **B. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.** COPD: chronic productive cough, frequent infections, rhonchi and hyperinflation.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has COPD after 40 pack-years of smoking. He has a productive cough most days and CT shows areas of alveolar destruction. He asks the student what COPD actually is. The student explains that two overlapping processes cause the persistent airflow limitation.
questions.q: Which pair best describes these processes?
questions.e: COPD = persistent airflow limitation from chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Why not Asthma and bronchiectasis? Separate diseases.

steps.x: COPD's two processes.
**C. Chronic bronchitis and emphysema.** COPD = persistent airflow limitation from chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has 1 year of breathlessness on exertion and morning cough. She has smoked 30 pack-years. Her spirometry after salbutamol shows FEV1 1.9 L (72% predicted), FVC 3.0 L, FEV1/FVC 0.63.

visual.title: FEV1, % predicted
visual.label: FEV1 72%
visual.caption: Stage by post-bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted once FEV1/FVC is below 0.7.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: COPD stage 2: FEV1 50-80% predicted with breathlessness on exertion. Why not COPD, mild (stage 1)? Stage 1 needs FEV1 above 80% predicted.

steps.x: Ratio below 0.7, FEV1 72% predicted.

elim: Fixed obstruction in a smoker with no atopy.
The ratio is reduced, not normal.

steps.x: **C. COPD, moderate (stage 2).** COPD stage 2: FEV1 50-80% predicted with breathlessness on exertion.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with COPD is brought in by her husband because she has become increasingly sleepy since yesterday. She has a bounding pulse and warm peripheries. Her oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air and her respiratory rate is 10 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on arterial blood gas?
o: Low pH with low PaCO2 and low bicarbonate
questions.e: Drowsy COPD patient + CO2 retention signs = type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis. Why not Low pH with low PaCO2 and low bicarbonate? Metabolic acidosis with compensation.

steps.x: Drowsy COPD patient, bounding pulse, warm hands, slow breathing.
**B. Low pH with raised PaCO2.** Drowsy COPD patient + CO2 retention signs = type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has breathlessness and a morning cough. He has smoked 35 pack-years. He has no history of asthma or atopy and his chest is hyperinflated with a prolonged expiratory phase. His GP suspects COPD and wants to confirm the diagnosis before starting treatment.
questions.q: Which result would confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 confirms COPD. Why not Hyperinflation on chest X-ray? Supportive but not diagnostic.

steps.x: Suspected COPD needs confirmation.
**C. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7.** Spirometry: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 confirms COPD.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with suspected COPD has a chest X-ray. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history and is breathless walking 50 metres. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air and his chest is hyperresonant with quiet breath sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Bilateral reticular shadowing at the bases
questions.e: COPD CXR: hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, more ribs visible, hyperlucent lungs. Why not Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy? Sarcoidosis.

steps.x: Long smoking history and suspected COPD.
**C. Flattened hemidiaphragms with hyperlucent lungs.** COPD CXR: hyperinflation, flat diaphragms, more ribs visible, hyperlucent lungs.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with severe COPD attends with a worse exacerbation. His oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air and he seems drowsy. His respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg. He has been using his salbutamol inhaler hourly.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: ABG in severe disease to look for raised CO2 and acidosis. Why not Chest X-ray only? Does not assess CO2.

steps.x: Severe, drowsy, low sats.

elim: Not useful in a drowsy COPD patient.
Not done in an acute exacerbation.

steps.x: **A. Arterial blood gas.** ABG in severe disease to look for raised CO2 and acidosis.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with COPD has full lung function tests. She has a 40 pack-year history and is breathless walking 100 metres. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.52. CT shows centrilobular emphysema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on gas transfer testing?
questions.e: Emphysema reduces DLCO through loss of alveolar surface. Why not Increased transfer factor? Seen in pulmonary haemorrhage.

steps.x: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls.

elim: Restrictive disease; COPD raises lung volumes.

steps.x: **E. Reduced transfer factor (DLCO).** Emphysema reduces DLCO through loss of alveolar surface.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with severe COPD and cor pulmonale has a 12-lead ECG. He has chronic hypoxia, ankle oedema and a raised JVP, and right ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiogram. He is in sinus rhythm.
questions.q: Which ECG finding is most likely?
o: P pulmonale in the inferior leads
ST elevation in V1 to V4
questions.e: COPD ECG: P pulmonale in inferior leads, right axis, low voltage, RBBB, MAT. Why not Delta waves? Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

steps.x: Chronic hypoxia, RV hypertrophy.
**C. P pulmonale in the inferior leads.** COPD ECG: P pulmonale in inferior leads, right axis, low voltage, RBBB, MAT.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with COPD has had one exacerbation in the last year, treated at home. His mMRC breathlessness score is 3 and he is breathless walking 100 metres on the flat. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.6 with FEV1 58% predicted. He has stopped smoking.
questions.q: Which GOLD group is he in?
questions.e: GOLD B = 0-1 exacerbations a year with more symptoms; offer pulmonary rehab from B up. Why not GOLD A? Group A has fewer symptoms.

clues: one exacerbation in the last year
steps.x: 0-1 exacerbations, more symptoms.

elim: C needs 2 or more exacerbations a year.
D needs 2 or more exacerbations a year with more symptoms.
A spirometric FEV1 stage, not a GOLD group.

steps.x: **B. GOLD B.** GOLD B = 0-1 exacerbations a year with more symptoms; offer pulmonary rehab from B up.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has COPD. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.48 and FEV1 is 26% predicted. She is breathless getting dressed and when sitting still. Her oxygen saturation is 90% breathing air. She stopped smoking 5 years ago.

visual.title: FEV1, % predicted
visual.label: FEV1 26%
visual.caption: Stage by post-bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted once FEV1/FVC is below 0.7.

questions.q: Which is her severity stage?
questions.e: Stage 4: FEV1 below 30% predicted, breathless at rest. Why not Stage 3 (severe)? Stage 3 is FEV1 30-50%.

steps.x: FEV1 below 30%, breathless at rest.
**D. Stage 4 (very severe).** Stage 4: FEV1 below 30% predicted, breathless at rest.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with newly diagnosed COPD has persistent breathlessness on SABA. He has stopped smoking and his inhaler technique is good. Before choosing his maintenance inhaler, his GP looks for features suggesting steroid responsiveness.
questions.q: Which finding most suggests steroid responsiveness?
o: FEV1 change of 100 mL after salbutamol
questions.e: Asthmatic features: atopy, high eosinophils, FEV1 variation 400 mL or more, diurnal PEF variation 20% or more. Why not FEV1 change of 100 mL after salbutamol? Below the 400 mL threshold.

steps.x: Choosing between LABA+LAMA and LABA+ICS.
**A. Diurnal peak flow variation of 25%.** Asthmatic features: atopy, high eosinophils, FEV1 variation 400 mL or more, diurnal PEF variation 20% or more.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with COPD has had three exacerbations needing oral steroids this year. She is breathless walking 100 metres (mMRC 3) and has a COPD Assessment Test score of 24. Post-bronchodilator FEV1 is 45% predicted. She has stopped smoking.
questions.q: Which GOLD group is she in?
questions.e: GOLD D = 2 or more exacerbations a year with more symptoms; offer pulmonary rehab. Why not GOLD C? C has 2 or more exacerbations but fewer symptoms.

steps.x: Two or more exacerbations and many symptoms.

elim: C has 2 or more exacerbations but fewer symptoms.
A spirometric stage, not a GOLD group.

steps.x: **D. GOLD D.** GOLD D = 2 or more exacerbations a year with more symptoms; offer pulmonary rehab.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man is diagnosed with mild COPD. He smokes 25 cigarettes a day. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.66 with FEV1 84% predicted. His oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. He asks which single measure will most improve his survival.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.e: Smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for survival in COPD. Why not Long-term oxygen therapy? Only for chronic hypoxaemia, and he must stop smoking first.

steps.x: Still smoking, asks about survival.

elim: Only for chronic hypoxaemia, and he must stop smoking first.
Does not improve survival in mild COPD.
Improves symptoms, but stopping smoking matters most.

steps.x: **E. Smoking cessation.** Smoking cessation is the most effective intervention for survival in COPD.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is newly diagnosed with COPD after spirometry. She has stopped smoking. She is breathless walking up hills and has had no exacerbations. She has no asthmatic features and her blood eosinophils are normal. Her oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: First-line: SABA (salbutamol) or SAMA (ipratropium) as needed. Why not LABA + ICS? Not first; and she has no asthmatic features.

steps.x: New COPD, mild symptoms.

elim: Not first; and she has no asthmatic features.

steps.x: **D. Short-acting bronchodilator as needed.** First-line: SABA (salbutamol) or SAMA (ipratropium) as needed.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with COPD remains breathless despite salbutamol as needed. He had asthma as a teenager, his blood eosinophils are 0.6 ×10⁹/L and his peak flow varies by 25% through the day. He has stopped smoking and his inhaler technique is good.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Steroid-responsive features: LABA + ICS instead of LABA + LAMA. Why not LABA + LAMA? First choice only when there are no asthmatic features.

steps.x: Asthmatic/steroid-responsive features.

elim: First choice only when there are no asthmatic features.
For frequent exacerbations after inhalers are optimised.

steps.x: **B. LABA + ICS.** Steroid-responsive features: LABA + ICS instead of LABA + LAMA.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with COPD takes a LABA + LAMA inhaler with good technique. She has had three exacerbations this year needing steroids and antibiotics, and her eosinophils are 0.4 ×10⁹/L. She has stopped smoking and attended pulmonary rehabilitation.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Triple therapy with LABA, LAMA and ICS
questions.e: Frequent exacerbations: triple therapy; warn that ICS raise pneumonia risk. Why not Add oral montelukast? Not part of COPD treatment.

steps.x: Frequent exacerbations on dual bronchodilators.
**E. Triple therapy with LABA, LAMA and ICS.** Frequent exacerbations: triple therapy; warn that ICS raise pneumonia risk.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with severe COPD has stopped smoking and completed pulmonary rehabilitation. CT shows emphysema mainly in both upper lobes. FEV1 is 28% predicted, PaCO2 5.9 kPa and TLCO 35% predicted.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Lung reduction surgery: upper lobe emphysema, FEV1 over 20%, PaCO2 under 7 kPa, TLCO over 20%. Why not Azithromycin prophylaxis? For frequent exacerbations, not upper lobe emphysema.

steps.x: Upper lobe emphysema, FEV1 above 20%, PaCO2 below 7, TLCO above 20%.

elim: For frequent exacerbations, not upper lobe emphysema.

steps.x: **E. Lung volume reduction surgery.** Lung reduction surgery: upper lobe emphysema, FEV1 over 20%, PaCO2 under 7 kPa, TLCO over 20%.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with COPD has had five exacerbations with sputum in the last year, one needing admission. She has stopped smoking, her inhalers are optimised and she completed pulmonary rehabilitation. Her doctor plans azithromycin 250 mg three times a week as prophylaxis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting?
questions.e: Check ECG (exclude long QT) and LFTs before azithromycin 250 mg three times a week. Why not Audiogram only? Hearing can be affected, but QT and LFTs are checked first.

steps.x: Before azithromycin.

elim: Hearing can be affected, but QT and LFTs are checked first.

steps.x: **C. ECG and liver function tests.** Check ECG (exclude long QT) and LFTs before azithromycin 250 mg three times a week.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with severe COPD stopped smoking 2 years ago. Two ABGs 3 weeks apart when stable show PaO2 7.6 and 7.7 kPa. He has ankle oedema and a raised JVP. His haemoglobin is 168 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: No oxygen: PaO2 is above 7.3 kPa
questions.e: LTOT: PaO2 below 7.3 kPa, or 7.3-8 kPa with oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension. Why not Ambulatory oxygen only? He meets criteria for long-term oxygen.

steps.x: PaO2 7.3-8 kPa with oedema, non-smoker.

elim: He meets criteria for long-term oxygen.
7.3-8 kPa with peripheral oedema still qualifies.

steps.x: **D. Long-term oxygen therapy.** LTOT: PaO2 below 7.3 kPa, or 7.3-8 kPa with oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with COPD has a PaO2 of 6.9 kPa on two stable ABGs 3 weeks apart. She has ankle oedema. She still smokes 10 cigarettes a day despite advice and smoking cessation support.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Withhold long-term oxygen until she stops smoking
questions.e: LTOT needs smoking cessation first; then 28% Venturi, target 88-92%. Why not Start long-term oxygen via 28% Venturi? She must stop smoking first: fire risk.

steps.x: Meets LTOT criteria but still smoking.

elim: She must stop smoking first: fire risk.

steps.x: **E. Withhold long-term oxygen until she stops smoking.** LTOT needs smoking cessation first; then 28% Venturi, target 88-92%.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with COPD has 4 days of worse breathlessness and green sputum. His oxygen saturation is 85% breathing air, temperature 37.8°C and respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute. He is allergic to penicillin. He is alert.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: High-flow oxygen, nebulisers, IV hydrocortisone, co-amoxiclav
questions.e: Exacerbation: SABA/SAMA, prednisolone 5 days, 88-92% oxygen, antibiotics (doxycycline/clarithromycin if penicillin allergic). Why not Controlled oxygen, nebulisers, prednisolone, amoxicillin? He is penicillin allergic.

steps.x: Exacerbation with infection, penicillin allergy.

elim: He needs steroids, oxygen and antibiotics.

steps.x: **B. Controlled oxygen, nebulisers, prednisolone, doxycycline.** Exacerbation: SABA/SAMA, prednisolone 5 days, 88-92% oxygen, antibiotics (doxycycline/clarithromycin if penicillin allergic).

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with COPD has an exacerbation. After 1 hour of controlled oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium and oral prednisolone, She is tired but alert. ABG shows pH 7.29, PaCO2 8.4 kPa and PaO2 8.0 kPa.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Type 2 respiratory failure with pH 7.25-7.35 = BiPAP. Why not Increase oxygen to 15 L/min? Will worsen hypercapnia.

steps.x: Persistent respiratory acidosis pH 7.25-7.35 despite treatment.
**D. Non-invasive ventilation.** Type 2 respiratory failure with pH 7.25-7.35 = BiPAP.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with COPD is ready to go home after an exacerbation. This is his third in a year. He has stopped smoking and has had his annual flu vaccine. His oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air and he is walking around the ward.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to his discharge plan?
o: Rescue pack of prednisolone and amoxicillin
questions.e: On discharge give a rescue pack (prednisolone and amoxicillin) and pulmonary rehab and vaccines. Why not Daily oral prednisolone long-term? Harmful.

steps.x: Discharge after exacerbation, frequent exacerbator.
**D. Rescue pack of prednisolone and amoxicillin.** On discharge give a rescue pack (prednisolone and amoxicillin) and pulmonary rehab and vaccines.

questions.stem: A 45 year old non-smoking man has basal panacinar emphysema on CT. His serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is very low. He is breathless walking 50 metres. A student asks how smoking causes emphysema in other patients.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism in smokers?
questions.e: Smoke drives neutrophil and macrophage inflammation; elastase overwhelms AAT and destroys septa. Why not Eosinophil degranulation in large airways? Asthma pathology.

clues: alpha-1 antitrypsin level is very low
steps.x: AAT deficiency and smoking share a protease-antiprotease imbalance.
**D. Neutrophil elastase overwhelming antiprotease defence.** Smoke drives neutrophil and macrophage inflammation; elastase overwhelms AAT and destroys septa.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with COPD coughs up sputum every morning. He has smoked 40 pack-years and has had a productive cough for 3 months of the year for the last 5 years. Bronchial biopsy shows enlarged submucosal mucous glands and goblet cell hyperplasia.
questions.q: Which process do these findings represent?
questions.e: Chronic bronchitis = chronic inflammation with mucus hypersecretion. Why not Asthma? Eosinophils and smooth muscle hypertrophy.

steps.x: Mucus gland hypertrophy and goblet cells.

elim: Alveolar wall destruction, not mucus gland change.

steps.x: **C. Chronic bronchitis.** Chronic bronchitis = chronic inflammation with mucus hypersecretion.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with emphysema has a chest X-ray showing flat hemidiaphragms and 8 anterior ribs visible. Her residual volume and total lung capacity are raised. She has smoked 45 pack-years and breathes out through pursed lips.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
o: Loss of elastic recoil causing airway collapse in expiration
questions.e: Lost elastic recoil makes airways collapse on expiration: gas trapping and hyperinflation. Why not Bronchial smooth muscle spasm? Reversible, asthma-type.

clues: residual volume and total lung capacity are raised
steps.x: Hyperinflation in emphysema.

elim: Would raise, not flatten, a hemidiaphragm.

steps.x: **C. Loss of elastic recoil causing airway collapse in expiration.** Lost elastic recoil makes airways collapse on expiration: gas trapping and hyperinflation.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with COPD and chronic hypoxia has ankle oedema and a raised JVP. His resting oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air. An echocardiogram shows raised pulmonary artery pressure and a thickened right ventricle.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Hypoxia constricts and remodels pulmonary vessels: pulmonary hypertension, RV hypertrophy. Why not Left ventricular failure? Left-sided disease.

steps.x: Chronic hypoxia and right-sided changes.
**A. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and remodelling.** Hypoxia constricts and remodels pulmonary vessels: pulmonary hypertension, RV hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with stable severe COPD has ABG showing pH 7.38, PaCO2 7.2 kPa and HCO3- 33 mmol/L. She is alert and at her usual level of breathlessness. A student asks why her pH is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Kidneys retain bicarbonate over days to normalise pH: compensated respiratory acidosis. Why not Hyperventilation? Would lower CO2.

steps.x: Chronic CO2 retention, raised bicarbonate, normal pH.
**C. Renal bicarbonate reabsorption over time.** Kidneys retain bicarbonate over days to normalise pH: compensated respiratory acidosis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with severe COPD and chronic CO2 retention is given 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask in the ambulance. His saturation rises to 99%, but he becomes drowsy and his PaCO2 rises sharply. The registrar explains why oxygen must be given carefully.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Some rely on hypoxic drive; keep sats 88-92%. Why not Increased carbon monoxide? Not from oxygen.

steps.x: Chronic CO2 retainer, PaCO2 rises on high oxygen.
**B. Loss of hypoxic respiratory drive.** Some rely on hypoxic drive; keep sats 88-92%.
